title: Milan after the Duomo: San Siro, Villa Necchi Campiglio and the Branca Tower, and which is worth the ticket
subtitle: A stadium, a house and a steel tower, all from the years between the wars, and one red metro line that joins them.
excerpt: What the San Siro stadium visit, Villa Necchi Campiglio and the Branca Tower in Parco Sempione each give you, who each one suits, what the tickets include, and how to see all three in a day by metro.

meta_title: San Siro, Villa Necchi, Branca Tower: worth the ticket?
meta_description: Three Milan visits after the Duomo: the San Siro stadium, Villa Necchi Campiglio and the Branca Tower. What each ticket includes and how to link them.

featured_image.alt: The San Siro stadium in Milan under a blue sky, with its spiral ramps, concrete towers and red roof girders

content_html:
[place attraction="villa-necchi-campiglio" city="milan"]

In 1933 Milan was getting ready for its fifth Triennale, the exhibition of design and architecture that had just moved into a new palace at the edge of Parco Sempione. The organisers wanted something tall beside it. The architect Gio Ponti gave them a tower of steel tubes, 108.6 metres high, and it was put up in about two and a half months.

On the other side of the centre, in those same years, the architect Piero Portaluppi was building a house with a heated swimming pool for a family that had made its money from sewing machines. And out to the west stood a football ground, opened in 1926, that would grow into the most famous stadium in Italy. All three can be visited today. Most people who come for the Duomo see none of them, so here is what each one gives you and which deserves your ticket.

San Siro: what the visit is

The stadium was paid for by Piero Pirelli, then president of AC Milan, and opened in September 1926. Inter moved in as well in 1947. Since 1980 its official name has been Stadio Giuseppe Meazza, after a forward who played for both clubs. The third tier, the eleven concrete towers with their spiral ramps and the red girders of the roof were added for the World Cup of 1990.

On a day without a match you can go in. The visit has two parts: a museum of the two clubs, with shirts, boots and trophies, and a walk through the building itself, to the changing rooms, the players' tunnel and the edge of the pitch, with a look at the empty stands from inside. Allow an hour to an hour and a half.

Two warnings. Tours do not run on match days, and they can stop the day before a big game or while a concert stage is being built, so check the calendar before you ride out. And the future of the stadium is no longer certain. In 2025 the city agreed to sell it to the two clubs, which plan a new ground next to it and the demolition of most of the old one when that is ready. That is some years off, but if you care about the place, do not put the visit off for long.

Villa Necchi Campiglio

The house stands at Via Mozart 14, in a quiet block behind Corso Venezia. Portaluppi built it between 1932 and 1935 for two sisters, Nedda and Gigina Necchi, and Gigina's husband, Angelo Campiglio. It had everything that was new: a lift, internal telephones, sliding doors that vanish into the walls, a veranda arranged as a winter garden, and a pool and a tennis court in the garden.

The last of the three owners died in 2001 and left the house to FAI, the Italian trust for historic places, which opened it in 2008. You see the family rooms, the bedrooms and bathrooms, the kitchens and the servants' quarters, with the furniture, the linen and the clothes still in place. Two collections of art given later hang on the walls. Allow an hour and a half with the garden. Entry is by time slot, and the house has usually been closed at the start of the week.

Villa Necchi Campiglio from the garden, with the pool. Photo: Dario Crespi, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The staircase designed by Piero Portaluppi. Photo: Palickap, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Branca Tower

Ponti's tower was closed in 1972 as unsafe and stood empty for thirty years. The Branca distillery paid for its restoration, and it reopened in 2002 under the company's name. A small lift, which holds only a handful of people, takes about a minute and a half to reach a glazed cabin at the top.

From there you look down on the park, the Sforza Castle and the Arco della Pace, across to the Duomo and the towers of Porta Nuova, and on a clear day to the Alps. The visit is short: you stay up for a few minutes and come down. The tower opens only on some days and for limited hours, and it closes in wind or bad weather.

The Branca Tower, seen from the paths of Parco Sempione. Photo: Fred Romero, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

From the top: the Arco della Pace at the edge of the park. Photo: Titus Grey, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Which is worth the ticket

  • You follow football: San Siro, without hesitation. For anyone else it is a long ride for a concrete building.
  • You like houses, design or the 1930s: Villa Necchi Campiglio. It is the one of the three that most visitors remember afterwards.
  • You want a view and have little time: the Branca Tower. It is the quickest of the three. The terraces of the Duomo give you the cathedral itself, the tower gives you the whole city with the cathedral in it.
  • You are with children: the tower and the park around it, then the stadium if they play.

What the partner's tickets include

  • The San Siro reserved entrance covers the museum and the walk through the stadium on your own, without a guide. The listing says the voucher is not valid on match days and that it is exchanged at the ticket office by gate 8. Bring an identity document.
  • The Villa Necchi Campiglio entry ticket covers the house and the garden at a chosen time, with texts and audio about the rooms on your own phone. Temporary exhibitions are listed as not included.
  • The Branca Tower entry ticket is the ride up and nothing else. The listing names three fixed times of day, one of them after dark, and repeats that the tower shuts in wind.
  • The two audio walks are commentary in the partner's app, with no entry anywhere. One follows fashion and design from Via Torino through the Galleria to the streets of the Quadrilatero. The other lists stops from the Duomo as far as San Siro, which is more than anyone covers on foot, so use it stop by stop.

These are the tickets and audio walks our partner sells for these places, with today's prices:

[partner city="milan" match="siro,necchi,branca,design" limit="5"]

Stringing them together by metro

The red line, M1, joins all three, with one change at the end.

  • Morning: Villa Necchi Campiglio. Get off at Palestro, or at San Babila. The house is five minutes away on foot.
  • Midday: the Branca Tower. Ride M1 from Palestro to Cadorna. The tower is ten minutes into the park, beside the Triennale.
  • Afternoon: San Siro. Back at Cadorna, take an M1 train towards Rho Fiera, not the Bisceglie branch, as far as Lotto. Change there to the lilac line, M5, and ride three stops to its terminus, San Siro Stadio. The station is at the stadium gates.

Fit the order to the time slots you were given. Current hours are on our page for Villa Necchi Campiglio.

From here

The Branca Tower leaves you in Parco Sempione, between the Triennale and the Sforza Castle, whose courtyards are free to walk through. From Villa Necchi, the shops of Corso Venezia and the public gardens are a few minutes away. See what else there is in Milan, or open the trip planner for Italy.

Cover photo: Jose Hidalgo, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

faqs.q: Is the San Siro stadium tour worth it?
faqs.a: For football followers, yes: you see the museum of the two clubs, the changing rooms, the tunnel and the pitch from the stands. If football does not interest you, Villa Necchi Campiglio or the Branca Tower is a better use of the time.

faqs.q: Can you visit San Siro on a match day?
faqs.a: No. The stadium visit does not run on match days, and it can also be suspended the day before a big game or around concerts. Check the calendar before you go.

faqs.q: Is Villa Necchi Campiglio worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you like houses and design. It is a villa of the early 1930s by Piero Portaluppi, shown with its furniture, bathrooms, kitchens and garden, and it takes about an hour and a half.

faqs.q: Can you go up the Branca Tower in Milan?
faqs.a: Yes. A small lift takes you to a cabin at the top of the 108.6 metre tower in Parco Sempione. It opens on some days only and closes in wind or bad weather.

faqs.q: How do you get to San Siro by metro?
faqs.a: Take the red line M1 towards Rho Fiera to Lotto, change to the lilac line M5 and ride to the terminus, San Siro Stadio, which is at the stadium gates.

title: Siena Cathedral: what the ticket covers, the Piccolomini Library, and what stays free on the Campo
subtitle: One cathedral, five doors with five ticket checks, a square that costs nothing and a synagogue two minutes behind it.
excerpt: What a Siena Cathedral ticket includes and what it leaves out (the museum, the crypt, the baptistery, the panorama), what the Piccolomini Library is, what is free and what is ticketed on Piazza del Campo, and how to visit the synagogue.
focus_keyword: Siena Cathedral ticket what is included
longtail_phrases: is the Piccolomini Library included in the Siena Cathedral ticket
what does the Siena Cathedral pass include
when is the floor of Siena Cathedral uncovered
is Piazza del Campo free
can you visit the synagogue in Siena
meta_title: Siena Cathedral ticket: what it covers, Piccolomini Library
meta_description: What a Siena Cathedral ticket includes, what needs the combined pass, when the floor is uncovered, what is free on the Campo, and the synagogue.

featured_image.alt: The striped marble front and bell tower of Siena Cathedral under a deep blue sky, with visitors on the square below

content_html:
[place attraction="siena-cathedral" city="siena"]

In 1339 the government of Siena decided that its cathedral, already one of the grandest in Tuscany, was too small. The plan was bold: build an enormous new nave at right angles to the old church, so that the whole existing cathedral would become nothing more than the transept of the new one. Work began at once. Nine years later the Black Death reached the city and killed a large part of its people. The money was gone, some of the new walls were found to be unsound, and the project was dropped.

What was built still stands beside the cathedral: a row of arches and one huge, empty end wall that the Sienese call the Facciatone, the big facade. It explains the layout you meet today. The cathedral is not one building with one door, but a cluster of separate places around a hill, each with its own ticket check. Knowing which ticket opens which door saves both money and a second trip to the desk.

The pieces of the cathedral complex

  • The cathedral itself, with the Piccolomini Library inside it.
  • The Museo dell'Opera, the cathedral museum, built into the abandoned nave. It holds Duccio's Maestà, the great altarpiece carried through the streets to the cathedral in 1311. From the museum a narrow stair climbs to the top of the Facciatone, sold as the Panorama.
  • The crypt, rooms under the choir with wall paintings of the thirteenth century, found again only in 1999.
  • The baptistery, lower down the hill behind the apse. Its font has bronze reliefs by Donatello, Ghiberti and Jacopo della Quercia.
  • The Gate of Heaven, a guided walk under the roof and along galleries above the nave, with its own ticket and fixed times.

The cathedral's own office sells a ticket for the church alone and a combined pass that adds the museum, the panorama, the crypt and the baptistery. The pass has been valid for more than one day. The roof walk is extra.

Inside the cathedral

The church is striped inside and out in white and dark green marble. Three things deserve your time.

The floor. Fifty-six panels of inlaid and engraved marble cover it from the door to the altar, made by about forty artists between the fourteenth and the nineteenth century. To protect them, most are kept under boards for much of the year. The whole floor has been uncovered for some weeks each year, usually in high summer and again from late summer into October, and the ticket has cost more in those weeks.

The pulpit. Nicola Pisano carved it in the 1260s, with crowded marble scenes of the life of Christ, on columns carried by lions.

The Piccolomini Library. A door in the left aisle leads to it. Cardinal Francesco Piccolomini had it built to honour his uncle, Pope Pius II, and to hold his books. He was elected pope himself in 1503 and died within a month. Pinturicchio and his workshop painted the room between 1502 and 1508 with ten scenes of the uncle's life, and the colours have hardly faded. Large choir books lie open in the cases. The room is small and is entered with the cathedral ticket, not a separate one.

Allow an hour for the cathedral and library. Shoulders and knees must be covered.

The Piccolomini Library, painted by Pinturicchio between 1502 and 1508. Photo: Helmut Aschauer, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

One of the fifty-six panels of the marble floor. Photo: Jordiferrer, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Campo: what is free

Five minutes downhill is Piazza del Campo, the shell-shaped square of brick, divided by lines of pale stone into nine segments for the Nine, the council that ruled Siena when it was laid out. Twice a summer, on 2 July and 16 August, the Palio is run around it: ten horses, three laps, about ninety seconds.

The square is free, and so is sitting on it, which is what everyone does. Two things on it need a ticket, both sold by the city and unrelated to the cathedral's tickets:

  • The Torre del Mangia, the tower of the town hall: about four hundred steps, limited numbers, no lift.
  • The Museo Civico, inside the town hall, with Ambrogio Lorenzetti's frescoes of good and bad government, painted in 1338 and 1339. That room has been under restoration, so ask whether it is open.

The Campo. Standing or sitting on it costs nothing. Photo: cisko66, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

The synagogue

Behind the town hall, in Vicolo delle Scotte, is the synagogue of Siena. Jews lived in the city from the Middle Ages. In 1571 Cosimo I de' Medici, the new ruler, confined them to a ghetto in these lanes. The synagogue was inaugurated in 1786, with a plain street front, as the rules required, and a bright interior between Rococo and Neoclassical. It is still used by the small community.

Visits take about half an hour and include a small Jewish museum. Opening days are limited, and it does not receive visitors on Saturdays or Jewish holidays, so check first.

The synagogue of 1786, a few steps behind the Campo. Photo: Sailko, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

What the partner's tickets cover

  • The Siena Cathedral and Piccolomini Library ticket with a city walk is entry to the cathedral and the library, "when available" in the listing's words, plus an audio walk through the streets in the partner's app. It is not the combined pass: the listing names the museum, the panorama, the crypt and the baptistery as excluded. You exchange the voucher for a paper ticket at a visitor centre in Via di Città and go in at the first free time. The walk has no commentary inside the church.
  • The Siena Synagogue entry ticket covers the synagogue and the Jewish museum.
  • The self-guided audio tour of Siena is the walk alone, from the Campo to the Medici Fortress. No entry is included.

If you want Duccio's Maestà and the view from the Facciatone, you need the combined pass from the cathedral's own office. These are the Siena tickets our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner city="siena" match="siena" limit="3"]

A day in order

Buses from Florence stop at the edge of the old town. The railway station is in the valley below, linked to the top by a long run of escalators. Start at the cathedral in the morning, before the day groups arrive. Walk down to the Campo for lunch, climb the tower or see the synagogue in the early afternoon, and keep the last hour for the square itself. Current hours are on our pages for Siena Cathedral and the Siena Synagogue.

From here

Opposite the cathedral door is Santa Maria della Scala, a hospital for pilgrims for about a thousand years and now a museum. The original carvings of the fountain on the Campo are kept there. See what else there is in Siena, or open the trip planner for Italy.

Cover photo: Spike, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is the Piccolomini Library included in the Siena Cathedral ticket?
faqs.a: Yes. The library is a room inside the cathedral and is entered with the cathedral ticket. It can be closed at times, which is why listings say "when available".

faqs.q: What does the Siena Cathedral combined pass include?
faqs.a: The cathedral with the Piccolomini Library, the Museo dell'Opera with the panorama from the Facciatone, the crypt and the baptistery. The Gate of Heaven roof walk is a separate ticket.

faqs.q: When is the floor of Siena Cathedral uncovered?
faqs.a: For some weeks each year, usually in high summer and again from late summer into October. The dates change every year, and the ticket has cost more in those weeks.

faqs.q: Is Piazza del Campo free?
faqs.a: Yes. The square is open at all hours and costs nothing. The Torre del Mangia and the Museo Civico in the town hall each need a ticket from the city.

faqs.q: Can you visit the synagogue in Siena?
faqs.a: Yes, on its opening days, with a ticket that also covers the small Jewish museum. It does not receive visitors on Saturdays or Jewish holidays.

title: Turin on foot: the royal squares, Palazzo Madama, and what is free under the arcades
subtitle: A capital built to be walked through in the dry: four squares, eighteen kilometres of arcades and one palace with two faces.
excerpt: A walking route through the royal squares of Turin, what Palazzo Madama is and whether to go in, what is free along the way (the Roman gate, the cathedral, the churches) and what needs a ticket, and what the partner sells.

what to see in Turin for free

meta_description: A walk through the royal squares of Turin: what Palazzo Madama holds, what is free under the arcades, what needs a ticket, and what the tickets include.

featured_image.alt: The Baroque stone front of Palazzo Madama in Turin, with tall windows, columns and statues along the roof, on Piazza Castello

content_html:
[place attraction="palazzo-madama-turin" city="turin"]

On 17 March 1861 the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in Turin. The deputies sat in Palazzo Carignano. The senators met three hundred metres away, in a hall on the first floor of Palazzo Madama. For four years this was the capital of the new country. Then the government left for Florence, and later for Rome, and Turin was left with the streets and squares of a capital and no court to fill them.

They had been built over two centuries by the dukes of Savoy, to one plan: straight streets, squares of equal fronts, and arcades along them, so that people could cross the centre in rain or snow without getting wet. About eighteen kilometres of arcades survive. The result is a city centre you can see almost entirely on foot, and much of it without a ticket. This is the route, and where paying is worth it.

The route in short

Piazza San Carlo, Piazza Carignano, Piazza Carlo Alberto, Piazza Castello with Palazzo Madama, the cathedral and the Roman gate, then down Via Po to the river. It is about three kilometres, flat, and takes two hours without going in anywhere. Coming from Porta Nuova station, you reach the first square in ten minutes under the arcades of Via Roma.

Piazza San Carlo and Piazza Carignano

Piazza San Carlo was laid out in the 1640s: a long rectangle of matching fronts over arcades, closed at one end by two churches that look like twins, Santa Cristina and San Carlo. In the middle rides Duke Emmanuel Philibert, sheathing his sword, a bronze of 1838. The old cafés under the arcades are part of the visit, and standing at the bar costs little.

Two minutes on is Piazza Carignano. Palazzo Carignano, begun in 1679 by Guarino Guarini, has a front of bare brick that curves in and out like a wave. Victor Emmanuel II, the first king of Italy, was born in it in 1820. It now holds the museum of the Risorgimento, with the chamber of the first parliament, on its own ticket. Behind it, on Piazza Carlo Alberto, is the palace's second front, added in the 1860s.

Piazza San Carlo, with the bronze horseman of 1838. Photo: Zairon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Piazza Castello and Palazzo Madama

Every main street leads to Piazza Castello. The Royal Palace closes its north side, behind a gate. In the middle, alone, stands Palazzo Madama, and it is worth walking right round it before anything else.

From the west it is a Baroque palace of pale stone with enormous windows. From the east it is a medieval castle of dark brick with round towers. Both are true. The building began as a gate of the Roman town. In the Middle Ages the gate was made into a fortress, and in the fifteenth century into a castle. In the seventeenth century two widowed duchesses, each ruling as regent and each known as Madama Reale, lived in it, which gave it its name. The second of them asked Filippo Juvarra for a new palace. Between 1718 and 1721 he built the front and the great double staircase behind it, and there the work stopped. The front was never given the building it was meant for.

What is inside

Since 1934 the palace has been the city's museum of older art, on four levels. The basement shows the Roman and medieval stonework. The ground floor has Gothic and Renaissance art, including the Portrait of a Man by Antonello da Messina, of 1476. The first floor has the Baroque rooms and the hall where the Senate met. The top floor has ceramics, glass, ivories and textiles. One of the towers has been open as a viewpoint, and there is a small medieval garden in the moat. Allow an hour and a half.

Is it worth the ticket? Yes, if you like buildings: you walk through two thousand years of one structure. If you want one large museum in Turin and only one, most people choose the Egyptian Museum, a few minutes away, which usually needs booking ahead.

The staircase Filippo Juvarra built behind the new front, 1718 to 1721. Photo: Marco Coïsson, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

What is free along the way

  • The squares and the arcades, at any hour.
  • The Porta Palatina, the brick gate of the Roman town, with two towers of sixteen sides, in a small park five minutes north of the cathedral.
  • The cathedral, finished in 1498 and the only Renaissance church in the city. The Shroud of Turin is kept here, in a closed case in a side chapel. It is shown to the public only on rare occasions, years apart, so what you see is the case and a copy.
  • The church of San Lorenzo on Piazza Castello, with no front to speak of and a dome by Guarini inside.
  • The Gran Madre di Dio, the round church of 1831 across the river, at the end of the walk.

One of the arcades of the centre. The city has about eighteen kilometres of them. Photo: Zairon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Porta Palatina, a gate of the Roman town. Free, at any hour. Photo: Jorge Franganillo, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

What needs a ticket

  • Palazzo Madama.
  • The Royal Museums: one ticket for the Royal Palace, the armoury, the picture gallery and Guarini's Chapel of the Shroud, which reopened in 2018 after a fire in 1997.
  • The Egyptian Museum.
  • The Mole Antonelliana: the glass lift to the viewing platform and the cinema museum below it, sold separately or together.
  • The museum of the Risorgimento in Palazzo Carignano.

Many museums here close one day a week, and the day differs from one to the next. Check it for each.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Palazzo Madama ticket is entry to the museum. The title says skip the line, and the instructions say to show the ticket at the desk by the entrance. A guided tour and an audio guide are listed as not included.
  • The audio walk through royal squares and landmarks follows almost exactly the route above, from Piazza San Carlo to the Gran Madre, by way of the Roman gate, the Royal Gardens and the Mole. It is commentary in the partner's app, with no entry anywhere.
  • The older audio tour of the city runs the other way, from the Porta Palatina to the Valentino Park. Its description quotes opening hours and ticket costs for the museums, written some time ago. Do not rely on them.

These are the Turin tickets and audio walks our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner city="turin" match="madama,turin" limit="3"]

From here

Via Po runs under arcades from Piazza Castello down to the river and the wide Piazza Vittorio Veneto. Across the bridge, a short climb from the Gran Madre leads to the Monte dei Cappuccini, a free terrace with the view of the city, the Mole and the Alps that is on every postcard. Hours for the palace are on our page for Palazzo Madama. See what else there is in Turin, or open the trip planner for Italy.

Cover photo: Federico Spadaro, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is Palazzo Madama in Turin worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you like buildings and decorative art. One visit takes you from a Roman gate and a medieval castle to a Baroque staircase by Filippo Juvarra, in about an hour and a half.

faqs.q: What can you see in Turin for free?
faqs.a: The royal squares and the arcades, the Roman Porta Palatina, the cathedral, the church of San Lorenzo, the Gran Madre di Dio and the view from the Monte dei Cappuccini.

faqs.q: How long does it take to walk the centre of Turin?
faqs.a: About two hours for the three kilometres from Piazza San Carlo to the river, without going into any museum. Add an hour and a half for Palazzo Madama.

faqs.q: Can you see the Shroud of Turin?
faqs.a: Not the cloth itself. It is kept in a closed case in the cathedral and shown only on rare occasions, years apart. Visitors see the case and a copy.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Palazzo Madama and the Royal Palace in Turin?
faqs.a: They are two buildings on the same square with separate tickets. Palazzo Madama is the city museum of older art. The Royal Palace is part of the Royal Museums, with the royal apartments, the armoury and the picture gallery.

title: Seville beyond the cathedral and the Alcázar: the Setas, Triana, Italica, and the city by bike
subtitle: A wooden roof you can walk on, a quarter across the river that costs nothing, a Roman city a bus ride away, and the flattest cycling in Spain.

featured_image.alt: The wooden lattice canopy of the Setas de Sevilla rising on thick trunks above a square, against a clear blue sky

content_html:
[place attraction="metropol-parasol" city="seville"]

For most of the twentieth century the Plaza de la Encarnación held the central food market of Seville. The old market hall was pulled down in 1973, with a promise of a new one, and the traders were moved to temporary stalls on a corner of the site. They stayed there for more than thirty years. When the city finally dug the square for an underground car park in the 1990s, the diggers hit Roman houses, with mosaics, and the car park was abandoned.

The answer came from a competition won in 2004 by the German architect Jürgen Mayer: six giant parasols of laminated timber, joined into one canopy about 150 metres long, with the ruins kept below, the market back at street level and a walkway on the roof. It opened in 2011, late and well over budget. Its official name is Metropol Parasol. Seville took one look and called it Las Setas, the mushrooms. It is the best place to begin a day that leaves the cathedral and the Alcázar behind.

The Setas: what the ticket gives you

Three of its levels cost nothing. The market under the canopy sells fish, ham and fruit in the mornings. Above it, a raised square in the shade of the timber is open to everyone. Around the edges are cafés.

The ticket is for the top: a lift from the basement takes you to a winding walkway across the roof, with a viewpoint about 28 metres above the street. Seville is a low city, so that is enough to see the cathedral, the Giralda and the roofs in every direction. The ticket has also included a short film and, after dark, a light show on the canopy. Go in the last hour of daylight and you get both views. In the basement, the Roman remains are shown in a museum called the Antiquarium, which has had its own entrance and hours.

Is it worth it? For the view at sunset, yes. At midday in summer the walkway has no shade, and the free levels are the better part.

Under the Setas. The square below the canopy is open to all. Photo: Benjamin Smith, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Triana, across the river

Triana was the quarter of sailors, potters and Roma families, and it still thinks of itself as a separate town. You reach it by the Isabel II bridge, iron arches of 1852 that replaced a bridge of boats in use since the twelfth century. Nearly everything here is free.

  • The market, at the end of the bridge, stands on the remains of the Castle of San Jorge, seat of the Inquisition in Seville from 1481. The ruins below it have been shown as a small museum.
  • Calle Betis, the riverside street, has the view back to the Torre del Oro and the bullring.
  • The church of Santa Ana, begun in the 1270s, is the oldest parish church in the city.
  • The ceramic workshops around Calle San Jorge and Calle Alfarería made the tiles you saw in the Alcázar. The Centro Cerámica Triana, in an old factory with its kilns, is the one stop that needs a ticket.

Allow two hours, more if you stay to eat. Triana is at its best in the evening.

The Isabel II bridge of 1852, known to everyone as the Triana bridge. Photo: Anual, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Italica, a Roman city by bus

In 206 BC the Roman general Scipio settled wounded soldiers on a hill above the river, nine kilometres north of where Seville now stands. The town was named Italica. Three centuries later it gave Rome an emperor, Trajan, who was born there, and his successor Hadrian, whose family came from it, rebuilt it on a grand scale.

What you walk through is Hadrian's new quarter: wide paved streets, the floors of large houses with mosaics still in place (look for the planets and the birds), and an amphitheatre that held about 25,000 people. Its arena served as the Dragonpit in the television series Game of Thrones.

The site is in the village of Santiponce. A suburban bus leaves from the Plaza de Armas bus station and takes about half an hour. Entry has been free for citizens of the European Union, with a small charge for others. The site has been closed on Mondays and keeps short hours in summer. There is almost no shade, so go early and take water. Allow two hours on site.

The amphitheatre of Italica, at Santiponce. Photo: Diego Delso, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The city by bike

Seville is flat and dry, and from 2007 the city built a network of separated cycle lanes, surfaced in green, that now covers well over a hundred kilometres. It changed how the city moves, and it makes a bike the easy way to join the places that are far apart on foot: the river bank, María Luisa Park and Plaza de España, Triana, and the Cartuja island.

You can rent from shops in the centre or use the public hire bikes. Stay on the lanes, which run on the pavement side and cross at their own lights. In the lanes of Santa Cruz, get off and walk. In July and August, ride before eleven or after seven.

A separated cycle lane and a rack of the city hire bikes. Photo: Frobles, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Two smaller tickets

Bucarelli Palace, in Calle Santa Clara in the north of the old town, is a seventeenth-century house still lived in by the family that owns it. The listing covers the ground floor.

Nao Vigía is a tethered balloon beside the Isla Mágica theme park on the Cartuja island, which the listing says rises up to 150 metres. The ticket does not include the park. Balloons of this kind stay down in wind, so check that it is flying.

What the partner's listings include

  • The Setas ticket with a city audio tour is entry to the Setas and an audio walk from there to the Alcázar by way of the bullring, the Torre del Oro and Plaza de España. The listing says there is no commentary inside the Setas.
  • The Italica audio tour is commentary only, told by a character from the television series. Entry to the site and the bus are yours to arrange.
  • Sevilla by bike is an audio route in the partner's app. The bicycle is not included.
  • The audio tour through art and legends is a long walk from Santa Cruz that crosses into Triana and ends on the Cartuja island. No entry is included.
  • Bucarelli Palace and Nao Vigía are plain entry tickets.

These are the tickets and audio tours our partner sells for this side of Seville, with today's prices:

From here

A good order for one day: Italica in the morning, the bike or a rest in the afternoon, the Setas for the last light and Triana for dinner. Current hours are on our page for the Setas. See what else there is in Seville, or open the trip planner for Spain.

faqs.q: Are the Setas de Sevilla worth it?
faqs.a: For the view near sunset, yes. The ticket takes you to a walkway on the roof, about 28 metres up. The market and the shaded square under the canopy are free.

faqs.q: What is there to see in Triana?
faqs.a: The Isabel II bridge, the market on the site of the Castle of San Jorge, the riverside Calle Betis, the church of Santa Ana and the ceramic workshops. Almost all of it is free.

faqs.q: How do you get to Italica from Seville?
faqs.a: By suburban bus from the Plaza de Armas bus station to Santiponce, about half an hour away. The site is at the edge of the village.

faqs.q: Is Italica free?
faqs.a: Entry has been free for citizens of the European Union, with a small charge for other visitors. The site has been closed on Mondays.

faqs.q: Is Seville good for cycling?
faqs.a: Yes. The city is flat and has a wide network of separated cycle lanes built from 2007. Avoid the middle of the day in summer, and walk the bike in the narrow lanes of Santa Cruz.

title: Riga on foot: the Art Nouveau quarter, Alberta iela and the old town, and what needs a ticket
subtitle: The best thing in Riga is a street of house fronts, and looking at it is free. So is most of the old town.
excerpt: Where the Art Nouveau houses of Riga are and which to look for on Alberta iela, how to walk from there to the old town, what is free, which few places charge for entry, and what the audio walks our partner sells do and do not include.

featured_image.alt: The blue and white Art Nouveau front of Elizabetes iela 10b in Riga, with two long sculpted faces at the top

content_html:
[place attraction="rigas-art-nouveau-center" city="riga"]

Around 1900 Riga was one of the largest ports of the Russian Empire, and it was growing faster than it could house its people. In the fifteen years before the First World War the fields beyond the old ramparts filled with blocks of flats, five and six storeys high, built for rent. The fashion of those years was Art Nouveau, and Riga built in it on a scale that few cities matched: more than eight hundred buildings, about a third of the centre.

The most extravagant of them were drawn by a man who was not trained as an architect. Mikhail Eisenstein was a civil engineer in the provincial administration, who designed fronts for wealthy clients on the side. His son Sergei, born in Riga in 1898, became the film director of Battleship Potemkin and wrote unkindly about his father's taste. The houses outlasted the opinion. They are the reason to come, and seeing them costs nothing.

Where the Art Nouveau quarter is

Not in the old town. The quarter lies about fifteen minutes on foot to the north, across the canal and the parks that replaced the ramparts. Three streets hold the best of it: Alberta iela, Elizabetes iela and Strēlnieku iela. Iela means street. The whole district is one block deep and can be seen in an hour.

Alberta iela, house by house

The street is named after Bishop Albert, who founded Riga in 1201, and it was built up in a few years after 1900. Stand in the middle and look up, since the best of it is above the second floor.

  • Numbers 2, 2a, 4, 6 and 8, a row on one side, are all by Eisenstein, from 1903 to 1906. Look for the sphinxes at the door of 2a and the top of its front, which rises a full storey above the roof with nothing behind it but sky.
  • Number 13, on the opposite corner, is Eisenstein again, from 1904: masks, screaming faces and long-necked women.
  • Number 12, from 1903, was built by the Latvian architect Konstantīns Pēkšēns for himself. It holds the museum.
  • Number 11, of 1908, is the opposite manner: grey, steep-roofed, almost without sculpture. This is National Romanticism, the style Latvian architects set against the imported ornament.

Round the corner, Strēlnieku iela 4a is a blue and white Eisenstein of 1905. Elizabetes iela 10b, two minutes away, is his best-known front, with two enormous faces at the top.

Alberta iela 13, by Mikhail Eisenstein, 1904. Photo: Diego Delso, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The one ticket here: the Art Nouveau museum

The Riga Art Nouveau museum opened in 2009 in the flat Pēkšēns lived in, on the ground floor of Alberta iela 12. The entrance is round the corner, in Strēlnieku iela. It is a furnished apartment of about 1903, with a dining room, a bedroom, a kitchen and a bathroom, and staff in the dress of the time. The spiral staircase of the house, painted on the underside all the way up, is the most photographed interior in Riga.

Half an hour is enough. It is worth the small charge if you want to know what was behind the fronts. If you only want the fronts, skip it.

The staircase of Alberta iela 12, the house of the Art Nouveau museum. Photo: Virtual-Pano, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Walking to the old town

From Elizabetes iela, cross the park along the canal. You come out at the Freedom Monument, a column of 1935 paid for by public donations, with a woman at the top holding up three stars. A guard of honour stands at its foot in daytime. The old town begins on the far side of the bridge.

The old town: what is free

Old Riga is small, about a kilometre from end to end, and closed to most traffic. Two hours cover it. Without paying you can see:

  • The Town Hall Square, with the House of the Blackheads. The guild house of unmarried foreign merchants, first built in 1334, was ruined in the war in 1941 and cleared away afterwards. What stands today is a rebuilding finished in 1999.
  • The Three Brothers in Mazā Pils iela, three houses side by side. The white one, from about 1490, is the oldest house in the city.
  • The Swedish Gate of 1698, cut through a house in the town wall, and the round Powder Tower.
  • The Cat House in Meistaru iela, of 1909, with two black cats on its turrets.
  • Dome Square and the outside of the cathedral.
  • The Central Market, just south of the old town, in five hangars built for Zeppelin airships and moved here in the 1920s.

The House of the Blackheads, rebuilt in the 1990s. Photo: Jorge Láscar, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The Three Brothers. The white one is the oldest. Photo: giggel, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

What needs a ticket

  • St Peter's Church. The ticket is for the church and the lift up its steeple to a gallery at about 72 metres, the best view over the old town.
  • Riga Cathedral. Entry is charged outside services. Its organ of 1884 has more than 6,700 pipes, and short concerts are sold separately.
  • The House of the Blackheads, for the halls inside and the medieval cellars.
  • The Art Nouveau museum and the national art museum.

Rules and charges at the smaller museums change, so check each one before you plan around it.

What the partner sells: audio walks only

Our partner sells no entry ticket in Riga. Its six listings are all self-guided audio walks: commentary and a map in the partner's app, on your own phone, with your own earphones. Each listing says that tickets to places on the way are not included.

  • Two Art Nouveau walks, about an hour each, start at the national art museum and end at the museum in Alberta iela. Their descriptions are almost the same, so one is enough.
  • The medieval old town tour starts at the Freedom Monument and takes about two hours past the castle and the three main churches.
  • Old town treasures runs from the Town Hall Square to the Three Brothers.
  • Old town and freedom covers similar ground with more stops. Its listed length is far longer than the others, so read it before choosing.
  • Whispers of history is the shortest old town walk, ending at the Freedom Monument.

A full day on foot: the Art Nouveau streets in the morning light, the park and the monument, the old town after lunch, St Peter's steeple towards evening. See what else there is in Riga, or open the trip planner for Latvia.

faqs.q: Where is the Art Nouveau district in Riga?
faqs.a: About fifteen minutes on foot north of the old town, across the canal and the parks. The best streets are Alberta iela, Elizabetes iela and Strēlnieku iela.

faqs.q: Is the Riga Art Nouveau museum worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want to see an interior: it is a furnished flat of about 1903 at Alberta iela 12, with a famous spiral staircase, and takes half an hour. The house fronts outside are free.

faqs.q: What is free to see in Riga?
faqs.a: The Art Nouveau streets, the Freedom Monument, the Town Hall Square, the Three Brothers, the Swedish Gate, the Cat House, Dome Square and the Central Market.

faqs.q: How long does it take to walk the old town of Riga?
faqs.a: About two hours without going in anywhere. Add an hour for the Art Nouveau quarter, which is a fifteen-minute walk away.

faqs.q: Who designed the Art Nouveau buildings in Riga?
faqs.a: Many architects. The most decorated fronts, on Alberta iela and Elizabetes iela, are by Mikhail Eisenstein, father of the film director Sergei Eisenstein. Latvian architects such as Konstantīns Pēkšēns and Eižens Laube built in a plainer style.
